perspective:
I, Mason Hurley, have access to the following information:

- I work as an accountant at a small community center. Martha Moua is a personal care aide there. We are colleagues with a mainly professional, not close, relationship.
- I reviewed financial reports and noticed discrepancies: healthcare expenses seemed unusually high and did not match usual spending patterns. This made me suspect Martha might be mismanaging funds, and I felt suspicious and anxious.
- I spoke with Martha about the report. I told her the numbers didn’t add up and pointed to the high healthcare expenses. Martha said there was likely a reasonable explanation or misentry and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing the report with Martha, I concluded the discrepancies were due to a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. I felt relieved but embarrassed.
- I told Martha I appreciated her quick clarification and said it seemed to be a clerical error. I apologized for my initial suspicion and for not asking her first. Martha said it was okay, errors happen, she was glad we cleared it up, and she understood I was being thorough. She suggested double-checking entries next time.
- I came to believe Martha is competent. I believed the recurring clerical errors pointed to inadequate financial management systems, not Martha’s management. I felt frustrated with the system but empathetic toward Martha.
- I discussed preventing future errors with Martha. I said the issue was not her management but the current system. I suggested proposing a new, more robust financial system, said I would draft a proposal, and asked for her input. Martha agreed and offered to help make sure it addressed the gaps we identified.
- I finished drafting the proposal for a new financial system. I believed it would benefit our operations, but I was uncertain whether management would approve or implement it.
- I told Martha I had finished the draft, believed it would benefit operations, and was not sure how management would receive it. Martha said it was solid and we should present it confidently. I agreed to prepare a detailed presentation and asked her to help gather data to strengthen our case. She agreed to help ensure we had the facts.
- After presenting the proposal to management, I felt satisfied with my efforts but physically and mentally exhausted. I believed I had done everything possible.
- I told Martha the presentation went well and that it was now up to management. Martha praised my work and suggested I take time off. I thanked her, said I would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped we would return to good news. Martha told me to enjoy my break and let her know if I needed anything.
